Some responses are one of several classes: the habitat an animal was found
in, a vegetation cover class, a damage score from 1 to 4. When the classes
have no order, tulpa fits a baseline-category (multinomial) logit model. When
they are ordered, it fits a cumulative-logit (proportional-odds) model, which
uses the order and needs fewer parameters. This article fits both to simulated
data with known coefficients, reads the coefficients and cutpoints with their
intervals, plots predicted class probabilities across a covariate, checks the
predicted class frequencies against the observed ones, and compares each model
with a simpler one. It ends with guidance on sparse classes and on when the
ordinal model is the wrong choice. Installation is covered in
[Get started](tulpa.html). The comparisons with MASS's `polr()` and nnet's
`multinom()` run only when those packages are installed.

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(tulpa)
```

## Two models for a categorical response

Index the observations by $i = 1, \ldots, n$ and the response classes by
$k = 1, \ldots, K$, with $K \ge 3$. Let $y_i$ denote the class of
observation $i$, $x_i$ its vector of covariates, and $p_{ik} = P(y_i = k)$
the probability of class $k$ for that observation.

The baseline-category logit takes class $K$ as the reference and gives every
other class its own linear predictor,

$$
\log \frac{p_{ik}}{p_{iK}} \;=\; \alpha_k + x_i^\top \beta_k,
\qquad k = 1, \ldots, K - 1,
$$

where $\alpha_k$ is the intercept of class $k$ and $\beta_k$ its vector of
covariate effects, both measured against the baseline. Solving for the
probabilities gives

$$
p_{ik} \;=\; \frac{\exp(\alpha_k + x_i^\top \beta_k)}
{1 + \sum_{l=1}^{K-1} \exp(\alpha_l + x_i^\top \beta_l)},
$$

with $\alpha_K = 0$ and $\beta_K = 0$. A model with $p$ covariates therefore
has $(K - 1)(p + 1)$ parameters. A coefficient $\beta_{kj}$ is the change in
the log odds of class $k$ against the baseline per unit of covariate $j$, so
its value depends on which class is the baseline; the probabilities do not.
tulpa uses the last level of the response factor as the baseline.

The cumulative logit uses the order of the classes. It models the probability
of falling at or below each class,

$$
P(y_i \le k) \;=\; \operatorname{logit}^{-1}\!\left(c_k - x_i^\top \beta\right),
\qquad k = 1, \ldots, K - 1,
$$

where $c_1 < c_2 < \cdots < c_{K-1}$ are the cutpoints and $\beta$ is one
vector of covariate effects shared by every class boundary. The class
probabilities are the differences
$p_{ik} = P(y_i \le k) - P(y_i \le k - 1)$, with $P(y_i \le 0) = 0$ and
$P(y_i \le K) = 1$. There is no intercept: the cutpoints carry the level. A
positive $\beta_j$ moves the whole distribution toward the higher classes,
and $\exp(\beta_j)$ is the factor by which the odds of being above any
boundary change per unit of covariate $j$. That this factor is the same at
every boundary is the proportional-odds assumption. The model has
$p + K - 1$ parameters.

Both fitters place a Gaussian prior with mean zero on every coefficient
(standard deviation 2.5 by default, set through `beta_prior`), find the
posterior mode by Newton's method (multinomial) or L-BFGS (ordinal), and
summarise the posterior by a Laplace approximation at that mode. The ordinal
fitter works on $c_1$ and the logs of the cutpoint increments, which keeps
the cutpoints ordered, and maps its draws back to cutpoints. Each fit takes a
fraction of a second on the data below.

## Unordered classes: the multinomial model

### Simulating habitat choice

The first dataset records in which of three habitats, forest, grassland or
wetland, each of 600 animals was found. Two standardised covariates describe
the site: `elev`, its elevation, and `water`, its distance to open water.
Wetland is the baseline. Against wetland, forest becomes more likely with
elevation and with distance from water, and grassland mostly with distance
from water.

```{r sim-multinomial}
set.seed(1)
n_h   <- 600
elev  <- rnorm(n_h)
water <- rnorm(n_h)
eta_f <- 0.4 + 1.2 * elev + 0.8 * water   # forest vs wetland
eta_g <- 0.6 + 0.3 * elev + 1.0 * water   # grassland vs wetland
P_h   <- cbind(exp(eta_f), exp(eta_g), 1)
P_h   <- P_h / rowSums(P_h)
hab_lev <- c("forest", "grassland", "wetland")
habitat <- apply(P_h, 1, function(p) sample(hab_lev, 1, prob = p))
dh <- data.frame(habitat = factor(habitat, levels = hab_lev),
                 elev = elev, water = water)
table(dh$habitat)
```

The levels are set explicitly so that wetland is last and becomes the
baseline. Each class has at least 100 observations.

### Fitting

`tulpa()` fits the model when `family = "multinomial"` and the response is a
factor. It hands the fit to `tulpa_multinomial()`, which can also be called
directly with the same formula and data.

```{r fit-multinomial}
fm <- tulpa(habitat ~ elev + water, data = dh, family = "multinomial")
fm
```

The coefficients are named `class:term`, and each one is a contrast with
wetland. `summary()` adds the posterior standard deviations and 95% credible
intervals.

```{r summary-multinomial}
coef(summary(fm))
```

All six simulated values (intercepts 0.4 and 0.6, slopes 1.2, 0.8, 0.3 and
1.0) lie inside their intervals. The farthest from its simulated value is the
forest elevation slope, 1.42 against 1.2, about 1.5 posterior standard
deviations away. `confint()` returns the same bounds as a matrix.

```{r confint-multinomial}
round(confint(fm), 3)
```

### Predicted probabilities across elevation

A coefficient against the baseline is hard to read on its own, because
raising one class's logit lowers the probability of every other class. The
class probabilities answer the question directly. `predict()` with
`type = "response"` returns one column per class, and `se.fit = TRUE` adds the
posterior standard deviation and the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of each
probability, computed over the fit's 2000 posterior draws. The grid below
varies elevation and holds distance to water at its mean.

```{r predict-multinomial}
nd_h <- data.frame(elev = seq(-2.5, 2.5, length.out = 60), water = 0)
pr_h <- predict(fm, newdata = nd_h, type = "response", se.fit = TRUE)
round(head(pr_h$fit, 3), 3)
```

Each row of `pr_h$fit` sums to one. The function below draws one line and one
credible band per class; it is reused for the ordinal model later.

```{r plot-helper}
plot_class_probs <- function(xg, pr, xlab, cols, ltys) {
  plot(range(xg), c(0, 1), type = "n", xlab = xlab,
       ylab = "predicted probability")
  for (k in seq_len(ncol(pr$fit))) {
    polygon(c(xg, rev(xg)), c(pr$lower[, k], rev(pr$upper[, k])),
            col = adjustcolor(cols[k], 0.25), border = NA)
    lines(xg, pr$fit[, k], col = cols[k], lty = ltys[k], lwd = 2)
  }
  legend("top", colnames(pr$fit), col = cols, lty = ltys, lwd = 2,
         horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
}
```

```{r plot-multinomial, fig.alt = "Predicted probabilities of forest, grassland and wetland against elevation with 95 percent credible bands: wetland falls and forest rises with elevation, grassland peaks near the middle"}
cols3 <- c("darkgreen", "goldenrod3", "steelblue")
plot_class_probs(nd_h$elev, pr_h, "elevation (standardised)",
                 cols3, c(1, 2, 4))
```

Forest rises with elevation and wetland falls. Grassland first rises and then
falls, although its own slope against wetland is positive: above the middle
of the range forest gains faster and takes probability from it. The bands are
narrowest near elevation zero, where most sites are.

### Observed against predicted class frequencies

The first check compares the observed share of each class with the mean
fitted probability. `fitted()` returns the class probabilities of every
observation at the posterior mode.

```{r check-overall-multinomial}
rbind(observed  = prop.table(table(dh$habitat)),
      predicted = colMeans(fitted(fm)))
```

A model with an intercept per class reproduces the overall shares almost by
construction, so the check is more informative within ranges of a
covariate. The next chunk cuts elevation into five groups of 120 sites and
compares, in each group, the observed share of each class with the mean
fitted probability.

```{r check-binned-multinomial}
bin_h <- cut(dh$elev, quantile(dh$elev, 0:5 / 5), include.lowest = TRUE)
obs_h <- prop.table(table(bin_h, dh$habitat), 1)
fit_h <- apply(fitted(fm), 2, function(p) tapply(p, bin_h, mean))
mid_h <- tapply(dh$elev, bin_h, mean)
```

```{r plot-binned-multinomial, fig.alt = "Observed class shares in five elevation groups as points and mean fitted probabilities as lines for forest, grassland and wetland; the points lie close to the lines"}
matplot(mid_h, fit_h, type = "l", lty = c(1, 2, 4), lwd = 2, col = cols3,
        ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "elevation group (mean)",
        ylab = "share of sites")
matpoints(mid_h, obs_h, pch = c(16, 17, 15), col = cols3)
legend("top", hab_lev, col = cols3, pch = c(16, 17, 15), lty = c(1, 2, 4),
       horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

The observed shares (points) lie close to the fitted ones (lines) in every
group.

The formal check is posterior predictive. `posterior_predict()` draws one
class per observation for each posterior draw and returns the class indices.
Counting the classes in each replicated dataset gives a predictive
distribution for each class count, and the observed count should fall inside
its central 95% interval.

```{r ppc-multinomial}
yrep_h <- posterior_predict(fm, ndraws = 1000, seed = 2)
cnt_h  <- t(apply(yrep_h, 1, tabulate, nbins = 3))
colnames(cnt_h) <- hab_lev
rbind(observed = table(dh$habitat),
      apply(cnt_h, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975)))
```

Each observed count lies inside its interval. The same count can be taken
within each elevation group by subsetting the columns of `yrep_h`.

### Comparison with nnet

nnet's `multinom()` fits the same model by maximum likelihood and takes the
first level as its baseline. Reordering the levels so wetland comes first
puts both fits on the same baseline.

```{r nnet, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_nnet}
dh_nnet <- transform(dh, habitat = relevel(habitat, ref = "wetland"))
fn <- nnet::multinom(habitat ~ elev + water, data = dh_nnet, trace = FALSE)
round(rbind(nnet  = as.vector(t(coef(fn))),
            tulpa = unname(coef(fm))), 3)
```

The two rows hold the same six coefficients in the same order (forest
intercept, elevation, water, then grassland). They differ by less than 0.01,
and every tulpa estimate is the smaller in absolute value, as expected from
the prior with standard deviation 2.5, which pulls the estimates toward zero.

## Ordered classes: the cumulative logit model

### Simulating cover classes

The second dataset gives the cover of a plant species on 500 plots in four
ordered classes, sparse, low, medium and high. Cover rises with soil moisture
(`moist`, slope 0.9) and falls with grazing intensity (`graze`, slope -0.7).
The three cutpoints are -1.5, 0 and 1.6.

```{r sim-ordinal}
set.seed(3)
n_c   <- 500
moist <- rnorm(n_c)
graze <- rnorm(n_c)
cuts  <- c(-1.5, 0, 1.6)
eta_c <- 0.9 * moist - 0.7 * graze
F_c   <- plogis(outer(-eta_c, cuts, "+"))   # P(y <= k), one column per k
P_c   <- cbind(F_c, 1) - cbind(0, F_c)
cov_lev <- c("sparse", "low", "medium", "high")
cover <- apply(P_c, 1, function(p) sample(cov_lev, 1, prob = p))
dc <- data.frame(cover = factor(cover, levels = cov_lev, ordered = TRUE),
                 moist = moist, graze = graze)
table(dc$cover)
```

The response is an ordered factor, and the order of its levels is the order
the model uses.

### Fitting, coefficients and cutpoints

`family = "ordinal"` routes the fit to `tulpa_ordinal()`. An intercept in
the formula is dropped, since the cutpoints carry the level.

```{r fit-ordinal}
fo <- tulpa(cover ~ moist + graze, data = dc, family = "ordinal")
fo
```

`coef()` returns the covariate effects only, as `MASS::polr()` does. The
cutpoints are named after the two classes they separate (`sparse|low`), and
`summary()` and `confint()` report them together with the effects.

```{r summary-ordinal}
coef(summary(fo))
```

The moisture slope, 0.93 against a simulated 0.9, and the grazing slope,
-0.62 against -0.7, lie within one posterior standard deviation of their
simulated values. The outer cutpoints do too. The middle one, -0.22 against
a simulated 0, is about two standard deviations away and its interval just
excludes zero; `MASS::polr()` gives the same value on these data (below), so
the offset is a property of this sample. The cutpoint intervals come from the
draws mapped back to cutpoint space, so they need not be symmetric about the
estimate.

The slopes are read on the odds scale through `exp()`: one standard
deviation more moisture multiplies the odds of being above any class boundary
by the factor below, and the interval transforms with it.

```{r odds-ordinal}
round(exp(cbind(estimate = coef(fo), confint(fo)[names(coef(fo)), ])), 2)
```

### Predicted probabilities across moisture

The ordinal model's probabilities come out of the same `predict()` call. The
grid varies moisture and holds grazing at its mean.

```{r predict-ordinal}
nd_c <- data.frame(moist = seq(-2.5, 2.5, length.out = 60), graze = 0)
pr_c <- predict(fo, newdata = nd_c, type = "response", se.fit = TRUE)
```

```{r plot-ordinal, fig.alt = "Predicted probabilities of the four cover classes against soil moisture with 95 percent credible bands: sparse falls, high rises, low and medium peak in turn"}
cols4 <- c("tan4", "orange2", "olivedrab3", "darkgreen")
plot_class_probs(nd_c$moist, pr_c, "soil moisture (standardised)",
                 cols4, c(1, 2, 4, 5))
```

Under proportional odds the classes take turns: sparse falls, high rises, and
each middle class peaks between the two classes on either side of it. The
model can produce no other pattern from a single covariate, which is the
point of the guidance on proportional odds below.

### Observed against predicted class frequencies

The check is the same as for the multinomial model, by groups of moisture and
by posterior predictive counts.

```{r check-binned-ordinal}
bin_c <- cut(dc$moist, quantile(dc$moist, 0:5 / 5), include.lowest = TRUE)
obs_c <- prop.table(table(bin_c, dc$cover), 1)
fit_c <- apply(fitted(fo), 2, function(p) tapply(p, bin_c, mean))
mid_c <- tapply(dc$moist, bin_c, mean)
```

```{r plot-binned-ordinal, fig.alt = "Observed cover-class shares in five moisture groups as points and mean fitted probabilities as lines; the points lie close to the lines"}
matplot(mid_c, fit_c, type = "l", lty = c(1, 2, 4, 5), lwd = 2, col = cols4,
        ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "moisture group (mean)",
        ylab = "share of plots")
matpoints(mid_c, obs_c, pch = 15:18, col = cols4)
legend("top", cov_lev, col = cols4, pch = 15:18, lty = c(1, 2, 4, 5),
       horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

```{r ppc-ordinal}
yrep_c <- posterior_predict(fo, ndraws = 1000, seed = 4)
cnt_c  <- t(apply(yrep_c, 1, tabulate, nbins = 4))
colnames(cnt_c) <- cov_lev
rbind(observed = table(dc$cover),
      apply(cnt_c, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975)))
```

### Comparison with MASS

`MASS::polr()` fits the same proportional-odds model by maximum likelihood,
with the same sign convention, $P(y \le k) = \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(c_k -
x^\top \beta)$, and the same names for the cutpoints.

```{r polr, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_mass}
fp <- MASS::polr(cover ~ moist + graze, data = dc)
round(rbind(polr  = c(coef(fp), fp$zeta),
            tulpa = c(coef(fo), fo$cutpoints)), 3)
```

### A probit link

`family = "ordinal_probit"` replaces the logistic distribution function by
the standard normal one. The coefficients are then on the scale of a latent
normal variable with unit variance, and they come out smaller than the logit
ones by about the ratio of the two distributions' standard deviations,
$\pi / \sqrt{3} \approx 1.8$.

```{r fit-probit}
fo_pr <- tulpa(cover ~ moist + graze, data = dc, family = "ordinal_probit")
round(rbind(logit = coef(fo), probit = coef(fo_pr),
            ratio = coef(fo) / coef(fo_pr)), 3)
max(abs(fitted(fo) - fitted(fo_pr)))
```

The ratios are 1.7 and 1.8. The last line is the largest difference between
the two fits' class probabilities over all plots and classes, 0.022. The
data were simulated with the logit link, and the probit fit gives class
probabilities within that distance of the logit ones.

## Comparing models

### Dropping a covariate

Both fitters report a Laplace approximation to the log marginal likelihood,
which `logLik()` returns and `compare_models()` ranks with
`criterion = "loglik"`. They also store pointwise log-likelihoods at every
posterior draw, so `criterion = "waic"` works too. The first comparison drops
grazing from the ordinal model.

```{r compare-drop}
fo_m <- tulpa(cover ~ moist, data = dc, family = "ordinal")
compare_models(full = fo, moisture_only = fo_m, criterion = "waic")
compare_models(full = fo, moisture_only = fo_m, criterion = "loglik")
```

In the WAIC table `elpd` is the estimated expected log predictive density,
`delta` its difference from the best model and `se_diff` the standard error
of that difference. The full model ranks first on both criteria: by 22.8
units of elpd, about three standard errors of the difference, and by 22.2 on
the log marginal likelihood (-613.5 against -635.8).

### Ordinal against multinomial on the same ordered data

The multinomial model can be fitted to ordered data too: it ignores the order
and gives every class its own intercept and slopes, 9 parameters here against
the ordinal model's 5. On data that satisfy proportional odds, the extra
parameters buy nothing.

```{r compare-ord-multi}
dc_nom <- transform(dc, cover = factor(cover, ordered = FALSE))
fm_c <- tulpa(cover ~ moist + graze, data = dc_nom, family = "multinomial")
compare_models(ordinal = fo, multinomial = fm_c, criterion = "waic")
```

WAIC favours the ordinal model by 3.8 units of elpd, about 1.4 standard
errors of the difference: the multinomial model predicts no better and
spends 9 effective parameters (`p_eff`) where the ordinal model spends 5.
The log marginal likelihood is less suited to this comparison:
the two models put different priors on different parameters (a ridge on the
class intercepts in one, on the log cutpoint increments in the other), and
the evidence depends on those priors directly.

### When proportional odds fails

The ordinal model shifts the whole distribution in one direction per
covariate. A covariate that makes the extreme classes more likely at one end
of its range and the middle class at the other has no such direction. The
next dataset has three ordered classes, and `x` lowers the logits of both
`low` and `high` against `mid` by the same amount.

```{r sim-nonpo}
set.seed(5)
n_x <- 500
xx  <- rnorm(n_x)
eta_x <- -0.3 - 1.2 * xx                 # low vs mid, and high vs mid
P_x <- cbind(exp(eta_x), 1, exp(eta_x))
P_x <- P_x / rowSums(P_x)
yx  <- apply(P_x, 1, function(p) sample(c("low", "mid", "high"), 1, prob = p))
dx  <- data.frame(y = factor(yx, levels = c("low", "mid", "high")), x = xx)
fo_x <- tulpa(y ~ x, data = transform(dx, y = as.ordered(y)),
              family = "ordinal")
fm_x <- tulpa(y ~ x, data = dx, family = "multinomial")
coef(summary(fo_x))["x", ]
compare_models(ordinal = fo_x, multinomial = fm_x, criterion = "waic")
```

The ordinal slope on `x` is -0.06 with an interval from -0.23 to 0.10,
although `x` changes the class probabilities strongly, and WAIC prefers the
multinomial model by 52 units of elpd, about 5.6 standard errors of the
difference. An ordinal slope near zero is therefore
not evidence that a covariate has no effect; refit the multinomial model and
compare before reading it that way.

## Sparse and empty classes

A class with few observations makes its own parameters uncertain. In the
ordinal model that is the cutpoint next to the rare class; in the
multinomial model it is the whole coefficient vector of that class. The
cover data below are simulated as before, but with a top cutpoint of 3.5, so
that the high class is rare.

```{r sim-sparse}
set.seed(7)
cuts_s <- c(-1.5, 0, 3.5)
F_s <- plogis(outer(-eta_c, cuts_s, "+"))
P_s <- cbind(F_s, 1) - cbind(0, F_s)
cover_s <- apply(P_s, 1, function(p) sample(cov_lev, 1, prob = p))
dc_s <- transform(dc, cover = factor(cover_s, levels = cov_lev,
                                     ordered = TRUE))
table(dc_s$cover)
fo_s <- tulpa(cover ~ moist + graze, data = dc_s, family = "ordinal")
coef(summary(fo_s))[, c("estimate", "std.error")]
```

The high class now has 29 plots. The slopes keep about the precision they had
on the first cover data (posterior standard deviations near 0.10 against
0.09), since every observation informs them. The standard deviation of the
top cutpoint, 0.23, is about twice that of the other two.

A class with no observations at all has no information about its
parameters, and both fitters refuse it by name. This happens most often after
subsetting, when a factor keeps a level none of the remaining rows have. The
subset below keeps the plots below high cover, for an analysis of the lower
classes alone.

```{r empty-level, error = TRUE}
dc_low <- subset(dc_s, cover != "high")
table(dc_low$cover)
tulpa(cover ~ moist + graze, data = dc_low, family = "ordinal")
```

The message names two remedies, dropping the level or merging it into a
neighbouring one. Here the high class was removed on purpose, so
`droplevels()` is the fix, and the model is fitted on the three classes that
remain, with two cutpoints.

```{r empty-level-fix}
fo_low <- tulpa(cover ~ moist + graze, data = droplevels(dc_low),
                family = "ordinal")
fo_low$cutpoints
```

The prior matters most where a class is sparse. Its standard deviation is
set with `beta_prior = list(mean = 0, sd = ...)`; the cutpoint prior of the
ordinal model with `cut_prior_sd` in `tulpa_ordinal()`. On the multinomial
habitat data, keeping only 12 wetland sites makes wetland the sparse
baseline. The fits below compare the default prior with a wider and a
narrower one.

```{r prior-sparse}
set.seed(7)
keep <- dh$habitat != "wetland" |
  seq_len(n_h) %in% sample(which(dh$habitat == "wetland"), 12)
dh_s <- dh[keep, ]
fits_s <- lapply(c(1, 2.5, 10), function(s) {
  tulpa(habitat ~ elev + water, data = dh_s, family = "multinomial",
        beta_prior = list(mean = 0, sd = s))
})
round(sapply(fits_s, coef), 2)
```

The columns are prior standard deviations 1, 2.5 and 10. With 12 sites of
one class every contrast with it depends on the prior: the forest intercept
moves from 2.38 to 3.01 between the narrowest and the widest prior, and the
forest elevation slope from 1.26 to 1.62 (simulated 1.2). On the full data
the default prior and nnet's unpenalised fit differed by less than 0.01.

## Practical guidance

| Response | Model | Parameters with $p$ covariates and $K$ classes |
|---|---|---|
| Unordered classes | `family = "multinomial"` | $(K - 1)(p + 1)$ |
| Ordered classes, effects in one direction | `family = "ordinal"` | $p + K - 1$ |
| Ordered classes, a covariate favouring the middle or both ends | `family = "multinomial"` | $(K - 1)(p + 1)$ |
| Two classes | `family = "binomial"` | $p + 1$ |

- Use the ordinal model when the order is real and the effects point one
  way. It estimates one slope per covariate instead of $K - 1$: on the cover
  data it needed 5 parameters where the multinomial model needed 9, and WAIC
  ranked it first by 3.8 units of elpd.
- Do not use the ordinal model when a covariate favours the middle class or
  both extremes. On the data simulated that way above, the ordinal slope was
  -0.06 with an interval covering zero, and WAIC preferred the multinomial
  model by 52 units of elpd. Fit both and compare with `criterion = "waic"`
  whenever the direction of an effect is in doubt.
- Count observations per class, not only in total. With 29 of 500 plots in
  the top cover class, the top cutpoint had a posterior standard deviation of
  0.23, about twice that of the other cutpoints, while the slopes kept their
  precision. In the multinomial model a sparse class carries $p + 1$ weakly
  informed parameters, and with 12 wetland sites out of 446 the forest
  intercept moved from 2.38 to 3.01 between prior standard deviations of 1
  and 10. At that size, report the prior with the estimates.
- Choose the baseline of the multinomial model on purpose. The coefficients
  are contrasts with the last level, and a well-observed class makes them
  easier to estimate. Reorder the levels with `factor(..., levels = )` before
  fitting. Without a prior the predicted probabilities would not depend on
  this choice; the prior on the contrasts makes them depend on it slightly.
- Merge or drop empty classes before fitting. Both fitters refuse a level
  with no observations, and the message names the level.
- Compare the two model types by WAIC, and models of one type by either
  criterion. The log marginal likelihood depends on the priors, which differ
  between the two types.

### What is supported

Both families are fixed-effect models. `tulpa()` refuses random effects,
smoothers and spatial or temporal fields for a categorical response, and it
fits by the Laplace driver only, so `mode` accepts `"auto"`, `"structured"`
or `"laplace"`.

```{r unsupported, error = TRUE}
dc_g <- transform(dc, site = rep(1:25, each = 20))
tulpa(cover ~ moist + (1 | site), data = dc_g, family = "ordinal")
```
